transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, honestly, it's just... I'm a mess right now. Ever since those foreclosure notices started showing up in the mail, I feel like I'm coming apart at the seams. I mean, I'm sitting in my truck crying before I even walk into the shop. And the shop, you know, it's loud, but lately, I'm jumping out of my skin every time the shop phone rings. I've been snapping at the apprentices, too. Poor kids, they don't know what they're doing half the time anyway. Like yesterday, this one kid, Tommy, he put the wrong grade oil in a front loader. A front loader! Can you believe that? I had to drain the whole thing. It took hours. But anyway, I'm making stupid mistakes myself in the repair bay, things I never would've done before. I just... I can't seem to keep my head on straight.
Have you been avoiding going to the shop or any other places because of how you've been feeling?

Well, I haven't exactly been avoiding the shop, but they... they actually pulled me out of the high-risk repair bay. My boss said I was too distracted, which, you know, is fair, but it still stings. I've been doing this for twenty years. I remember when I first started, I was the only woman in the shop, and I had to prove I could handle the big rigs just as well as the guys. I worked twice as hard. I even bought my own set of pneumatic tools before I was officially off probation just to show I was serious. Cost me a fortune back then. 

But outside of work, yeah, I guess I have been avoiding things. I used to volunteer at church every Sunday, setting up the coffee and donuts. Mrs. Higgins always complains if the decaf isn't ready by 9 AM sharp. She's a sweet lady, but very particular about her decaf. And I haven't been to my fitness classes in weeks. I used to love the kickboxing one, the instructor, Dave, always played the best 80s rock playlists. I even stopped going to my truck-club outings. We were supposed to go off-roading up near the old quarry last weekend, but I just... I couldn't bring myself to go. I just sit at home now, staring at that pile of mail.
Have you experienced any moments where you felt detached from yourself or your surroundings?

Detached? Like... like I'm outside my body or spaced out like that? No, no, I don't think so. I know exactly where I am, it's just that everything feels so heavy right now. I'm definitely in my own skin. 

Though, speaking of my surroundings... my house is just a total disaster lately. I usually keep things so neat, especially my kitchen. I have this gorgeous vintage 1950s diner-style table in there—cherry red vinyl chairs, chrome trim, the whole nine yards. I actually found it at a swap meet a few years back. The guy wanted three hundred bucks for it, but I talked him down to one-fifty because the chrome on the legs was all pitted and rusted. I spent an entire Sunday afternoon polishing it with fine-grade steel wool and Coca-Cola. It's an old mechanic's trick, you know? The phosphoric acid in the soda just eats right through the surface rust without scratching the metal. It came out looking brand new, honestly. 

But anyway... now you can't even see that table. The shiny part, I mean. It's completely buried under all those bank notices and bills. I haven't even been able to sit there to eat a bowl of cereal. Just piles and piles of paper staring at me. But... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, feeling detached. No, I haven't had anything like that happen. Just... just the stress of it all.
Have you been having trouble sleeping lately?

Sleep? Oh man, my sleep is completely wrecked. I try to get into bed around ten, because my shift at the shop starts at six, but I just lay there staring at the ceiling. Sometimes I hear the neighbor's dog barking. It's this little beagle mix, cute thing, really floppy ears. They named him Buster. Buster is a terrible name for a beagle, if you ask me. I had a beagle growing up named Tracker, which makes a lot more sense, right? Because they track things with their noses. We used to take Tracker out to the woods behind my grandpa's house, and he'd just go wild sniffing every single tree stump. My grandpa actually built this incredible wooden doghouse for him, hand-carved the shingles and everything. He was a carpenter, my grandpa. Could build a whole house from scratch. I think that's where I get my mechanical skills from, honestly. He taught me how to use a hammer before I could even ride a bike. 

But yeah, sleep. I don't know, I just... I can't turn my brain off. I'm tossing and turning all night, and when I finally do drift off, it's already time to get up.
Have you been experiencing any feelings of fear or apprehension about the future?

Fear about the future? I don't... I don't really know if fear is the right word. I just don't know what's going to happen. It's like everything is up in the air right now. 

Speaking of being up in the air, we used to have this old hydraulic lift at the shop, the one in bay three. It was a total nightmare. The safety catch would always stick, so you'd have this massive eighteen-wheeler hovering over your head, and you're just praying the hydraulics don't give out. I actually brought my own jack stands in for a while just to be safe. You can never be too careful with those heavy rigs. I remember this one time, a guy named Earl—he retired a few years back, moved down to Florida to fish, I think—he was working under a Peterbilt and the lift actually dropped an inch. Just one inch, but the sound it made... sounded like a gunshot echoing through the garage. Scared the living daylights out of everyone. We all stopped what we were doing. Earl just slid out on his creeper, white as a sheet, and went on his lunch break two hours early. I don't blame him. 

But, um... what was I saying? The future. Right. I just... I haven't really thought that far ahead, honestly. I'm just trying to get through the day without losing my mind over all those bills on the table.
Have you been feeling anxious most of the time since you started receiving the foreclosure notices?

Anxious? I mean, yeah, I guess so. It's hard not to be when every time the mail carrier comes, my stomach does a backflip. I actually know our mail carrier pretty well. His name is Dan, nice guy, always wears those little blue shorts even when it's freezing out. I don't know how he does it. He told me once he used to run cross-country in high school, so maybe his legs just don't feel the cold anymore. He drives one of those Grumman LLVs, you know, the standard mail trucks? They're fascinating little machines, built on a Chevy S-10 chassis with an aluminum body so they don't rust. The problem with them, though, is the engine block. They use this old Iron Duke four-cylinder, which is practically indestructible, but they have a terrible tendency to catch fire because the windshield washer fluid line runs right over the fuse box. I actually offered to reroute it for Dan once, just as a favor, because I'd hate to see him go up in flames on his route. He just laughed, probably thought I was joking, but I was dead serious. It's a thirty-minute fix, tops. 

But anyway, anxious. Yeah. Every time I see his truck pull up, I just feel this knot in my chest, wondering if he's dropping off another one of those letters. I just... I don't know how to fix this.
Have you been feeling guilty about your current situation or like you're a failure in any way?

Guilty? Um... I don't know if guilt is it. I mean, I guess I just feel like I'm stuck, you know? Like I'm spinning my wheels in the mud and not getting anywhere. 

Speaking of mud, you wouldn't believe the state some of these rigs come into the shop. Last week, this guy brought in a front-end loader that looked like it had been submerged in a swamp for a decade. The undercarriage was just caked in this thick, clay-like sludge. It took me three hours with the pressure washer just to find the grease zerks. And you have to be careful with those high-psi washers, too. If you hit a hydraulic line at the wrong angle, you can actually inject water right through the rubber casing. I saw a guy do that once, ruined a perfectly good hose. He was a rookie, though, didn't know any better. We called him "Sparky" because he managed to short out a battery terminal on his first day. Nice kid, but definitely not cut out for heavy machinery. He ended up leaving to work at a bakery or something. Honestly, sometimes I think about doing something like that. Just baking bread all day. It smells so good, right? Like yeast and flour. My grandma used to make this incredible sourdough... 

But, uh, what did you ask me? Oh, feeling like a failure. I just... I don't really think about it like that. I just want to figure out how to keep my house.
Do you often feel like you're worthless or a burden to others?

Worthless? A burden? I mean, I don't... I don't really feel like that. I'm just the one who usually takes care of things, you know? I fix things. That's what I do. 

Like this morning, my neighbor's lawnmower wouldn't start. It's this older John Deere riding mower, one of the good ones with the Kawasaki V-twin engine, not the cheap single-cylinders they put in the newer models you get at the big box stores. Anyway, he was out there pulling the cord on this other little push mower, looking completely defeated, so I walked over. Took me five minutes to realize his carburetor float was stuck. People always forget to use fuel stabilizer in the winter, and the ethanol in modern gas just turns to varnish. It gums up everything. I told him he needs to run it dry before he puts it in the shed for the season. I ended up pulling the carb off, spraying it down with some cleaner, and tapping the bowl with the handle of a screwdriver. Started right up on the first turn of the key. The sound of a healthy engine catching, it's just... it's a really satisfying sound. Sort of a deep, steady rumble. He tried to give me twenty bucks, but I told him to keep it. We've got to look out for each other, right? Especially nowadays. 

But, um... a burden. No, I don't think I'm a burden to anybody. I just... I really need to figure out this house situation before they actually change the locks.
Do you often feel hopeless about your situation?

Hopeless? Well, I wouldn't say hopeless. I mean, there's always a way to fix something, right? You just have to find the right tool for the job. 

Speaking of tools, I was at this estate sale over the weekend, just looking around, you know? And I found this incredible set of vintage Snap-on wrenches. The old ones, from the 70s, back when they actually stamped the date codes into the metal. They had this beautiful patina on them, not rusted, just... well-loved. The guy running the sale didn't even know what he had. He had them in a rusty old coffee can marked "misc tools - $5." Five bucks! I almost felt bad handing him the money. Almost. I took them home and spent a good hour just cleaning them up with some WD-40 and a brass wire brush. You have to be careful with steel brushes on old chrome, it'll scratch it right up and then you've ruined the finish. Brass is softer, so it takes the grime off without damaging the plating. It's the same principle we use when we're cleaning mating surfaces on engine blocks. You don't want to use anything harder than the metal you're working on, or you'll create low spots and the gasket won't seal right. We had this one guy at the shop, another rookie, who took a pneumatic die grinder with a Roloc disc to an aluminum cylinder head... absolute disaster. He took off so much material we had to send it out to a machine shop to get it decked. Cost the shop a fortune. 

But anyway, hopeless. No, I don't feel hopeless. I just need to figure out the right way to tackle this mortgage thing. There's got to be a way to sort it out, I just haven't found it yet.
Are there any specific thoughts or memories that you've been trying to avoid thinking about lately?

Avoid thinking about? Um... no, not really. I mean, I try not to dwell on the whole foreclosure notice thing, obviously, but there's no specific memory I'm running from. 

Although, speaking of running... my truck's transmission has been acting up lately. It's an older Allison 1000, usually bulletproof, you know? They put them in the heavy-duty Silverados. But it's been doing this weird hunting thing between third and fourth gear when it's cold. I pulled the pan this weekend to check the fluid, and it smelled a little burnt. Not terrible, but definitely past its prime. The magnet in the pan had some fine metallic sludge on it, which is normal wear and tear, but there were a couple of bigger flakes that I didn't love seeing. I'm hoping it's just a sticky solenoid. The A and B solenoids on those valve bodies can get gummed up if you don't stay on top of your fluid changes. It's a messy job, though. ATF gets everywhere. It's got this distinct smell, kind of sweet but also metallic. It takes days to wash it out of your skin, no matter how much Gojo you use. I actually prefer the citrus-scented hand cleaners, the ones with pumice in them. They really get into the cracks of your knuckles. 

But, uh, no. No memories I'm avoiding. Just trying to keep my head down and figure out the bank stuff.
Have you been feeling overwhelmed by your emotions most of the time since you started receiving the foreclosure notices?

Overwhelmed? Yeah. Yeah, I'd say that. Ever since those foreclosure notices started coming in the mail, I just... I feel like I'm coming apart at the seams. I'm sitting in my truck before work, just crying. I jump out of my skin every time the phone rings. I'm snapping at the apprentices at the shop, which isn't fair to them, and I'm making these stupid mistakes in the repair bay that I never, ever would have made before. 

Like yesterday, I was working on this Peterbilt 389. Beautiful truck. The owner operator had it all decked out with custom chrome and a long drop visor. He brought it in for a routine PM and a valve adjustment on his Cummins ISX15. Those overheads are critical on the ISX, especially if you want to avoid dropping a valve and destroying the whole block. The spec for the intake is fourteen thousandths, and the exhaust is twenty-seven thousandths. You have to use the barring tool to roll the engine over and get each cylinder to top dead center on the compression stroke before you set the lash. It's a precise process. You slide the feeler gauge in, and you want just a slight drag. Not too tight, not too loose. If it's too tight, the valve won't seat properly and it'll burn up. Too loose, and it's noisy and you lose power. Anyway, I was setting cylinder number four, and I completely forgot to tighten the jam nut on the rocker arm after I set the clearance. I just... forgot. I moved right on to the next cylinder. Thank god the shop foreman was walking by and noticed my torque wrench sitting on the cart untouched. If I had fired that engine up with a loose jam nut, the adjusting screw would have backed out, the pushrod could have bent, or worse. It would have been a catastrophic failure. Tens of thousands of dollars in damage, all because my brain was spinning about the bank taking my house instead of focusing on the engine right in front of me. 

So, yeah. I guess I am overwhelmed. It's just... it's a lot to carry around, you know?
Have you been feeling numb or disconnected from things that usually bring you joy or excitement?

Numb? Disconnected? I don't know, maybe not numb, exactly. I mean, I still get worked up about things. But joy? I haven't really felt excited about much of anything lately. It just feels like there's a heavy blanket over everything. 

Even my usual stuff... like, I usually love getting out to the salvage yards on a Saturday morning. You know, before it gets too hot, when the dew is still on the windshields of all those wrecked rigs. There's this one yard out past the county line, mostly commercial stuff, old Macks, Freightliners, some heavy equipment. I go out there looking for core parts to rebuild. Alternators, starter motors, that kind of thing. Last time I went, I spotted a Delco Remy 39MT starter just sitting in the mud under a scrapped Kenworth. Those are gear-reduction starters, incredibly torque-y, they use them on the big 15-liter diesels. Usually, you have to fight tooth and nail to get one off a block in the yard because everyone wants them. They're heavy, too, like forty pounds, so you're laying on your back in the dirt, wrestling this chunk of iron while trying not to strip the mounting bolts. You have to use a half-inch drive ratchet, usually with a cheater bar, because those bolts are torqued down to like 150 foot-pounds and they've been heat-cycled a million times. Anyway, I saw it sitting there, already pulled, and normally I'd be thrilled. It's an easy flip if you rebuild the solenoid and swap the brushes. But I just... I looked at it, and I didn't even care. I just walked right past it. Left a perfectly good, rebuildable 39MT in the mud because I just didn't have the energy to lug it to the front office. 

So, yeah. I guess I'm not really getting joy out of the things I usually like. Just can't seem to muster the interest.
Are you avoiding talking or thinking about something specific related to your foreclosure situation?

Specific? No, not really. I mean, the whole thing is just constantly in my face, so it's not like I'm hiding from one particular part of it. I talk to the bank when they call, I look at the papers... it's just a giant mess you have to dig through. 

Kind of like... well, speaking of digging through messes, I had to do a full chassis lube on a Cat 950M wheel loader yesterday. Massive machine, they use them in the rock quarries around here. And let me tell you, the engineers who design those things must absolutely hate mechanics. They hide the grease zerks for the steering cylinders so deep inside the articulation joint. You literally have to climb up into the center of the machine, straddling the main drive shaft, and you're just instantly covered in old grease and quarry dust. And if the operator hasn't been doing his daily walk-arounds, those zerks get completely buried in hardened mud. You have to sit there with a pocket pick and a can of brake cleaner just to dig the fitting out so the grease gun coupler will actually snap on. And you have to use a good heavy-duty lithium complex grease, usually with a high moly content, because those pivot points take a massive amount of shear stress when that loader is carrying a full bucket of crushed rock. If you skip it, the pin gets galled up, and then you're looking at having to bring in a specialist to line-bore the whole joint, which takes days and costs a fortune. So you just have to dig in and deal with the mess, no matter how much you don't want to. 

But, uh... sorry, what was I saying? Oh, right, the house stuff. Yeah, no, I'm not avoiding any specific thoughts or anything. It's all just one big headache I'm stuck dealing with.
Do you feel anxious when you're around other people, like at work or in social gatherings?

Anxious around other people? No, not really. I mean, I'm snapping at the apprentices, like I said, but that's just because my fuse is so short right now, not because they make me nervous. I've always been pretty comfortable around people, especially at the shop. It's a loud, chaotic environment, you know? Air compressors running, impacts hammering, radios blaring. You kind of have to yell just to be heard. 

Speaking of loud, we had this old Detroit Diesel Series 60 in the shop last week. A 12.7 liter, pre-EGR engine. Those things are legendary for being practically bulletproof, but man, they have a very distinct sound. People call it the "Detroit rattle." It's this sharp, clattering noise when they idle. Anyway, this guy brings his Freightliner Classic XL in, and the engine is just screaming. Sounded like someone threw a handful of bolts into a blender. Turned out, the bull gear in the front gear train was completely chewed up. The bull gear is this massive, heavy gear that drives the camshaft and the accessory drive. It's pressed onto a hub, and if the backlash isn't set perfectly when it's installed, or if the bearings start to fail, the teeth just grind themselves to dust. You have to pull the whole front cover off the engine, which means dropping the oil pan, pulling the radiator, the charge air cooler, the fan hub... it's a monumental job. And the whole time you're doing it, you're covered in this thick, black soot that just permeates your skin. You can wash your hands ten times with pumice soap and you'll still have a black ring around your fingernails for a week. 

But, uh, no. I don't feel anxious around people. Just tired. Just really, really tired of it all.
Are there any activities that you used to enjoy but have lost interest in since you started receiving the foreclosure notices?

Activities I used to enjoy? Yeah, I mean... pretty much all of them, honestly. I just don't have it in me right now. Like, I used to go to these fitness classes twice a week, and I was always volunteering at church, helping set up for events. And my truck club outings! We used to do these weekend meets, barbecue, talk shop... I haven't been to one in months. I just stopped showing up for all of it. 

Even at work, it's affecting me. They actually took me out of the high-risk repair bay. Which, honestly, I get. You can't be distracted when you're working under a suspended load or dealing with high-pressure hydraulics. Like last month, before they moved me, we had this massive excavator come in, a Hitachi ZX470. The boom cylinder was leaking hydraulic fluid everywhere. Now, to repack those cylinders, you're dealing with immense pressure. The hydraulic fluid in those systems can run upwards of 5,000 PSI. If you crack a fitting before relieving the pressure, that fluid can inject right through your skin, and then you're looking at emergency surgery to prevent amputation. It's no joke. You have to use these massive spanner wrenches to get the gland nut off the cylinder, and sometimes you have to heat it with an oxy-acetylene torch just to break the thread locker loose. And the seals themselves, the chevron packing, it's this incredibly stiff polyurethane. You have to soak them in hot oil just to make them pliable enough to stretch over the piston without tearing them. It's exacting work, and you really have to be on your game. 

But yeah, they moved me to the lighter stuff, doing basic PMs—preventative maintenance—on the smaller delivery box trucks. Oil changes, greasing chassis, checking brake pad thickness. It's boring, but I guess it's safer right now since my head's not fully in it. So, yeah, I've just dropped out of everything I used to do.
Have you been feeling this overwhelmed and anxious every day since you started receiving the foreclosure notices?

Every single day, yeah. It's been about four months now, right when those first notices started showing up in the mail. Just this constant weight on my chest, every morning I wake up. 

It reminds me of when we had to pull the transmission on an Allison 4500 RDS out of a refuse truck a few months back. Those garbage trucks, they just get beaten to death, stop-and-go all day, every day. The PTO—power take-off—is constantly engaging and disengaging to run the hydraulic compactor. Anyway, this thing came in and it wouldn't shift out of second gear. We dropped the pan, and the fluid looked like burnt coffee, full of clutch material. We had to drop the driveline, support the back of the engine, and use a heavy-duty transmission jack to lower this massive hunk of iron out from under the chassis. And when you crack the case open on an Allison, it's like a puzzle box of planetary gear sets, clutch packs, and the valve body. The valve body is the brain, full of these tiny little solenoids and shift valves. If even a speck of dirt gets in there, the valve sticks, and you lose a gear. We had to soak the whole assembly in solvent, blow out every single passage with compressed air, and test every solenoid with a multimeter to make sure the resistance was within spec. It's tedious, frustrating work, and you're just standing there under the lift for hours, your neck cramping up, transmission fluid dripping in your hair... 

But yeah, four months of this. Every day since the bank started sending those letters, I just feel completely overwhelmed.
Are you avoiding talking to anyone in particular about your foreclosure situation?

Avoiding anyone? Um... well, I haven't really told anyone at all, to be honest. It's not like I'm actively hiding from one specific person, I just... I don't want to talk about it with anyone. It's embarrassing, you know? 

Like, I don't want the guys at the shop knowing my business. We talk a lot of trash, but it's mostly about the equipment. Like yesterday, we were arguing over the best way to diagnose a DPF—diesel particulate filter—issue on a Cummins ISX15. Those things are a nightmare. The EPA regulations mandate all this aftertreatment stuff now, so you've got the DPF, the DOC, the SCR... it's a whole alphabet soup under the truck. Anyway, when a DPF clogs up with soot, the engine computer initiates an active regen, basically dumping raw fuel into the exhaust stream to burn the soot out. But if the seventh injector—the doser valve—is clogged, or if the differential pressure sensor is lying to the ECM, the regen fails, and the truck derates. It basically goes into limp mode, and the driver can't go over 5 miles an hour. So you hook up your laptop with the Cummins Insite software, and you're looking at all these parameters—exhaust gas temperatures, soot load percentages. Sometimes you have to force a parked regen, and the truck just sits there screaming at 1500 RPM for an hour, blowing out heat that could melt the asphalt. If that doesn't work, you have to physically pull the DPF down, which weighs like 80 pounds and is usually rusted solid to the v-band clamps, and send it out to be baked in a specialized kiln. It's a massive headache.

But yeah, I don't talk about the house stuff with them. Or my sister. Or anyone, really. I just keep it to myself.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite since you started receiving the foreclosure notices?

Changes in my appetite? Um... I don't think so. I haven't really noticed, honestly. I guess I'm eating about the same as usual. I still grab my regular sandwich from the lunch truck when it rolls into the yard every day. 

Actually, speaking of food trucks, we just had a massive refrigerated delivery truck in the shop a couple weeks ago that hauls for the local restaurants. A Freightliner M2 with a Thermo King T-880R reefer unit on the box. The driver came in panicking because the box wouldn't drop below 40 degrees, and he was hauling frozen seafood, so that's a huge liability. When you're dealing with those transport refrigeration units, it's a whole different ballgame than just heavy diesel. You're basically an HVAC tech on top of being a mechanic. 

I hooked up my manifold gauges to the suction and discharge service valves on the compressor, and the low-side pressure was pulling way down into a vacuum. That tells you right away there's either a massive leak in the system or a restriction. We had to break out the electronic leak detector and trace every single inch of the refrigerant lines. Turns out, the vibration from the road had caused a heavy wire loom to rub right through the liquid line going to the expansion valve. You can't just vent that stuff to fix it, either. You have to hook up a recovery machine and pull all the remaining R-404a refrigerant into a DOT-approved cylinder. If the EPA catches you venting hydrofluorocarbons, they will fine the shop tens of thousands of dollars. So you recover it, braze in a new section of copper tubing with a torch, swap out the liquid line filter drier, and then you have to pull a deep vacuum on the whole system with a two-stage pump down to like 500 microns to boil off any moisture before you can even think about weighing in the new charge. It took my entire shift just to get it blowing ice cold again. 

But, um... what were you asking? Oh, right, my eating. Yeah, no, my appetite is pretty much the same, I haven't noticed any changes there.
Are you avoiding talking to anyone in particular about your financial difficulties with the house?

Wait, didn't we just talk about that? Or... I guess you mean specifically about the money side of it. But yeah, like I said before, I'm not really hiding from anyone in particular. I just don't bring up the financial stuff or the house with anybody at all. It's just... money is so stressful right now. 

It's like that with the customers at the shop, too, honestly. Everyone's stressed about money and repair bills. We had this guy bring in a John Deere 544 wheel loader last week, and the main hydraulic implement pump was just whining like a banshee. When you're dealing with those variable displacement axial piston pumps, if the swashplate wears out or the brass slippers get scored up from contaminated fluid, the whole system just loses pressure. You try to curl a loaded bucket and it just completely stalls out. 

I had to tell the guy that to replace that pump, he was looking at easily eight, maybe ten grand just for the part alone. And getting it out is a total nightmare. You're belly-crawling under the cab, dealing with these massive high-pressure hydraulic lines. You have to be so careful, because if you don't bleed the residual pressure out of the accumulators first, that hydraulic fluid can shoot out and inject straight through your skin, which is a guaranteed trip to the ER and emergency surgery. We had to drain like fifty gallons of AW46 hydraulic oil into these massive drums, unbolt the drive shaft, and wrestle this eighty-pound hunk of steel out of the belly pan. And the whole time, the customer is standing around the bay complaining about our hourly labor rate. I'm just thinking, buddy, you want this thing lifting concrete jersey barriers or not? You can't cheap out on hydraulics. 

But, um... yeah. To answer your question again, no. I'm not avoiding anyone specifically about the finances. I just keep it all to myself.
Have you found it difficult to perform your job or maintain relationships since you started receiving the foreclosure notices?

Well, yeah, I guess it has been affecting things. Like at work, my foreman actually took me out of the high-risk repair bay recently. I guess I was just too distracted with the house stuff on my mind. And you really, really can't be distracted in the high-risk bay. That's where we handle the heavy suspension overhauls and the air brake chambers. 

People who just drive regular cars don't realize how dangerous commercial air brakes are. You've got these dual-chamber brake pots on the drive axles—one side is the service brake, and the other is the spring brake, which acts as the parking and emergency brake. There's a massive, heavy-duty steel coil spring inside that housing holding back like two or three thousand pounds of mechanical force. If you need to replace a ruptured rubber diaphragm inside, you absolutely have to manually cage that spring first. You use this special T-bolt that threads into the back of the chamber and compresses the spring safely. If you're not paying attention and you take off the metal clamp band while that spring is still under tension... man, that housing will explode like a literal bomb. It will take your head clean off your shoulders. We had a young tech a few years ago who didn't respect the spring tension, and the housing shot off and shattered his jaw and collarbone. So, you know, if your head isn't one hundred percent in the game, they won't let you near it. 

So I'm mostly just doing basic preventative maintenance right now. Oil changes, greasing chassis, that kind of thing. 

And outside of work... I don't know, I just don't have the energy for anyone. I've stopped showing up for my church volunteering, I dropped my fitness classes, and I haven't been to any of my truck-club outings either. We used to do these big weekend meetups, showing off custom glider kits. A lot of the folks run classic Peterbilt 389s with the extended hoods. You drop a pre-emission Caterpillar C15 engine in there, twin turbos, straight-pipe exhaust with eight-inch bullhauler stacks... they sound incredible when you hit the Jake brake coming down a grade. But I just haven't been going to those either. I just don't have it in me to keep up with any of it right now.

Well, I haven't exactly been avoiding the shop, but they... they actually pulled me out of the high-risk repair bay. My boss said I was too distracted, which, you know, is fair, but it still stings. I've been doing this for twenty years. I remember when I first started, I was the only woman in the shop, and I had to prove I could handle the big rigs just as well as the guys. I worked twice as hard. I even bought my own set of pneumatic tools before I was officially off probation just to show I was serious. Cost me a fortune back then. 

But outside of work, yeah, I guess I have been avoiding things. I used to volunteer at church every Sunday, setting up the coffee and donuts. Mrs. Higgins always complains if the decaf isn't ready by 9 AM sharp. She's a sweet lady, but very particular about her decaf. And I haven't been to my fitness classes in weeks. doctor.intent: determine presence of dissociative symptoms

patient.answer:
Detached? Like... like I'm outside my body or spaced out like that? No, no, I don't think so. I know exactly where I am, it's just that everything feels so heavy right now. I'm definitely in my own skin. 

Though, speaking of my surroundings... my house is just a total disaster lately. I usually keep things so neat, especially my kitchen. I have this gorgeous vintage 1950s diner-style table in there—cherry red vinyl chairs, chrome trim, the whole nine yards. I actually found it at a swap meet a few years back. The guy wanted three hundred bucks for it, but I talked him down to one-fifty because the chrome on the legs was all pitted and rusted. I spent an entire Sunday afternoon polishing it with fine-grade steel wool and Coca-Cola. It's an old mechanic's trick, you know? The phosphoric acid in the soda just eats right through the surface rust without scratching the metal. It came out looking brand new, honestly. 

But anyway... now you can't even see that table. The shiny part, I mean. It's completely buried under all those bank notices and bills. I haven't even been able to sit there to eat a bowl of cereal. Just piles and piles of paper staring at me. But... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, feeling detached. No, I haven't had anything like that happen. Just... just the stress of it all.

doctor.intent: determine presence of anxiety symptoms

Sleep? Oh man, my sleep is completely wrecked. I try to get into bed around ten, because my shift at the shop starts at six, but I just lay there staring at the ceiling. Sometimes I hear the neighbor's dog barking. It's this little beagle mix, cute thing, really floppy ears. They named him Buster. Buster is a terrible name for a beagle, if you ask me. I had a beagle growing up named Tracker, which makes a lot more sense, right? Because they track things with their noses. We used to take Tracker out to the woods behind my grandpa's house, and he'd just go wild sniffing every single tree stump. My grandpa actually built this incredible wooden doghouse for him, hand-carved the shingles and everything. He was a carpenter, my grandpa. Could build a whole house from scratch. I think that's where I get my mechanical skills from, honestly. He taught me how to use a hammer before I could even ride a bike. 

But yeah, sleep. I don't know, I just... I can't turn my brain off. I'm tossing and turning all night, and when I finally do drift off, it's already time to get up.

patient.answer:
Guilty? Um... I don't know if guilt is it. I mean, I guess I just feel like I'm stuck, you know? Like I'm spinning my wheels in the mud and not getting anywhere. 

Speaking of mud, you wouldn't believe the state some of these rigs come into the shop. Last week, this guy brought in a front-end loader that looked like it had been submerged in a swamp for a decade. The undercarriage was just caked in this thick, clay-like sludge. It took me three hours with the pressure washer just to find the grease zerks. And you have to be careful with those high-psi washers, too. If you hit a hydraulic line at the wrong angle, you can actually inject water right through the rubber casing. I saw a guy do that once, ruined a perfectly good hose. He was a rookie, though, didn't know any better. We called him "Sparky" because he managed to short out a battery terminal on his first day. Nice kid, but definitely not cut out for heavy machinery. He ended up leaving to work at a bakery or something. Honestly, sometimes I think about doing something like that. Just baking bread all day. It smells so good, right? Like yeast and flour. My grandma used to make this incredible sourdough... 

But, uh, what did you ask me? Oh, feeling like a failure. I just... I don't really think about it like that. I just want to figure out how to keep my house.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of persistent and pervasive feelings of worthlessness
doctor.question: Do you often feel like you're worthless or a burden to others?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of worthlessness or being a burden, which are typical symptoms of major depressive disorder. My symptom profile for Adjustment Disorder does not include these specific symptoms.

patient.answer:
Worthless? A burden? I mean, I don't... I don't really feel like that. I'm just the one who usually takes care of things, you know? I fix things. That's what I do. 

Like this morning, my neighbor's lawnmower wouldn't start. It's this older John Deere riding mower, one of the good ones with the Kawasaki V-twin engine, not the cheap single-cylinders they put in the newer models you get at the big box stores. Anyway, he was out there pulling the cord on this other little push mower, looking completely defeated, so I walked over. Took me five minutes to realize his carburetor float was stuck. People always forget to use fuel stabilizer in the winter, and the ethanol in modern gas just turns to varnish. It gums up everything. I told him he needs to run it dry before he puts it in the shed for the season. I ended up pulling the carb off, spraying it down with some cleaner, and tapping the bowl with the handle of a screwdriver. Started right up on the first turn of the key. The sound of a healthy engine catching, it's just... it's a really satisfying sound. Sort of a deep, steady rumble. He tried to give me twenty bucks, but I told him to keep it. We've got to look out for each other, right? Especially nowadays. 

But, um... a burden. No, I don't think I'm a burden to anybody. I just... I really need to figure out this house situation before they actually change the locks.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of persistent and pervasive feelings of hopelessness
doctor.question: Do you often feel hopeless about your situation?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of hopelessness, which is typically a symptom of depression. patient.answer:
Hopeless? Well, I wouldn't say hopeless. I mean, there's always a way to fix something, right? You just have to find the right tool for the job. 

Speaking of tools, I was at this estate sale over the weekend, just looking around, you know? And I found this incredible set of vintage Snap-on wrenches. The old ones, from the 70s, back when they actually stamped the date codes into the metal. They had this beautiful patina on them, not rusted, just... well-loved. The guy running the sale didn't even know what he had. He had them in a rusty old coffee can marked "misc tools - $5." Five bucks! I almost felt bad handing him the money. Almost. I took them home and spent a good hour just cleaning them up with some WD-40 and a brass wire brush. You have to be careful with steel brushes on old chrome, it'll scratch it right up and then you've ruined the finish. Brass is softer, so it takes the grime off without damaging the plating. It's the same principle we use when we're cleaning mating surfaces on engine blocks. You don't want to use anything harder than the metal you're working on, or you'll create low spots and the gasket won't seal right. We had this one guy at the shop, another rookie, who took a pneumatic die grinder with a Roloc disc to an aluminum cylinder head... absolute disaster. He took off so much material we had to send it out to a machine shop to get it decked. Cost the shop a fortune. 

But anyway, hopeless. No, I don't feel hopeless. I just need to figure out the right way to tackle this mortgage thing. There's got to be a way to sort it out, I just haven't found it yet.

patient.answer:
Avoid thinking about? Um... no, not really. I mean, I try not to dwell on the whole foreclosure notice thing, obviously, but there's no specific memory I'm running from. 

Although, speaking of running... my truck's transmission has been acting up lately. It's an older Allison 1000, usually bulletproof, you know? They put them in the heavy-duty Silverados. But it's been doing this weird hunting thing between third and fourth gear when it's cold. I pulled the pan this weekend to check the fluid, and it smelled a little burnt. Not terrible, but definitely past its prime. The magnet in the pan had some fine metallic sludge on it, which is normal wear and tear, but there were a couple of bigger flakes that I didn't love seeing. I'm hoping it's just a sticky solenoid. The A and B solenoids on those valve bodies can get gummed up if you don't stay on top of your fluid changes. It's a messy job, though. ATF gets everywhere. It's got this distinct smell, kind of sweet but also metallic. It takes days to wash it out of your skin, no matter how much Gojo you use. I actually prefer the citrus-scented hand cleaners, the ones with pumice in them. They really get into the cracks of your knuckles. 

But, uh, no. No memories I'm avoiding. Just trying to keep my head down and figure out the bank stuff.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient is experiencing significant emotional distress
doctor.question: Have you been feeling overwhelmed by your emotions most of the time since you started receiving the foreclosure notices?

target_item.name: Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response
target_item.manifestation: Ever since those foreclosure notices started coming, I feel like I’m coming apart at the seams—crying in my truck before work, jumping every time the phone rings, snapping at the apprentices, and making stupid mistakes in the repair bay that I never would’ve made before.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling overwhelmed by emotions in response to an identifiable stressor (the foreclosure notices), which corresponds directly to the 'Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response' symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Overwhelmed? Yeah. Yeah, I'd say that. Ever since those foreclosure notices started coming in the mail, I just... I feel like I'm coming apart at the seams. I'm sitting in my truck before work, just crying. I jump out of my skin every time the phone rings. I'm snapping at the apprentices at the shop, which isn't fair to them, and I'm making these stupid mistakes in the repair bay that I never, ever would have made before. 

Like yesterday, I was working on this Peterbilt 389. Beautiful truck. The owner operator had it all decked out with custom chrome and a long drop visor. He brought it in for a routine PM and a valve adjustment on his Cummins ISX15. Those overheads are critical on the ISX, especially if you want to avoid dropping a valve and destroying the whole block. The spec for the intake is fourteen thousandths, and the exhaust is twenty-seven thousandths. You have to use the barring tool to roll the engine over and get each cylinder to top dead center on the compression stroke before you set the lash. It's a precise process. You slide the feeler gauge in, and you want just a slight drag. Not too tight, not too loose. If it's too tight, the valve won't seat properly and it'll burn up. Too loose, and it's noisy and you lose power. Anyway, I was setting cylinder number four, and I completely forgot to tighten the jam nut on the rocker arm after I set the clearance. I just... forgot. I moved right on to the next cylinder. Thank god the shop foreman was walking by and noticed my torque wrench sitting on the cart untouched. If I had fired that engine up with a loose jam nut, the adjusting screw would have backed out, the pushrod could have bent, or worse. It would have been a catastrophic failure. Tens of thousands of dollars in damage, all because my brain was spinning about the bank taking my house instead of focusing on the engine right in front of me. 

So, yeah. I guess I am overwhelmed. It's just... it's a lot to carry around, you know?

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of significant emotional numbing or avoidance behaviors

My symptom profile does not include anhedonia or emotional numbing; it covers stress-related maladaptive response, additional requirements 1 and 2, functional impairment, and duration.

patient.answer:
Numb? Disconnected? I don't know, maybe not numb, exactly. I mean, I still get worked up about things. But joy? I haven't really felt excited about much of anything lately. It just feels like there's a heavy blanket over everything. 

Even my usual stuff... like, I usually love getting out to the salvage yards on a Saturday morning. You know, before it gets too hot, when the dew is still on the windshields of all those wrecked rigs. There's this one yard out past the county line, mostly commercial stuff, old Macks, Freightliners, some heavy equipment. I go out there looking for core parts to rebuild. Alternators, starter motors, that kind of thing. Last time I went, I spotted a Delco Remy 39MT starter just sitting in the mud under a scrapped Kenworth. Those are gear-reduction starters, incredibly torque-y, they use them on the big 15-liter diesels. Usually, you have to fight tooth and nail to get one off a block in the yard because everyone wants them. They're heavy, too, like forty pounds, so you're laying on your back in the dirt, wrestling this chunk of iron while trying not to strip the mounting bolts. You have to use a half-inch drive ratchet, usually with a cheater bar, because those bolts are torqued down to like 150 foot-pounds and they've been heat-cycled a million times. Anyway, I saw it sitting there, already pulled, and normally I'd be thrilled. It's an easy flip if you rebuild the solenoid and swap the brushes. But I just... I looked at it, and I didn't even care. I just walked right past it. Left a perfectly good, rebuildable 39MT in the mud because I just didn't have the energy to lug it to the front office. 

So, yeah. I guess I'm not really getting joy out of the things I usually like. Just can't seem to muster the interest.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of avoidance behaviors
doctor.question: Are you avoiding talking or thinking about something specific related to your foreclosure situation?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about avoidance of talking or thinking about the stressor (foreclosure), which is a symptom of PTSD (avoidance). My symptom profile covers Adjustment Disorder, specifically the maladaptive response, additional requirements regarding onset and offset, functional impairment, and duration. It does not include avoidance symptoms.

patient.answer:
Specific? No, not really. I mean, the whole thing is just constantly in my face, so it's not like I'm hiding from one particular part of it. I talk to the bank when they call, I look at the papers... it's just a giant mess you have to dig through. 

Kind of like... well, speaking of digging through messes, I had to do a full chassis lube on a Cat 950M wheel loader yesterday. Massive machine, they use them in the rock quarries around here. And let me tell you, the engineers who design those things must absolutely hate mechanics. They hide the grease zerks for the steering cylinders so deep inside the articulation joint. You literally have to climb up into the center of the machine, straddling the main drive shaft, and you're just instantly covered in old grease and quarry dust. And if the operator hasn't been doing his daily walk-arounds, those zerks get completely buried in hardened mud. You have to sit there with a pocket pick and a can of brake cleaner just to dig the fitting out so the grease gun coupler will actually snap on. And you have to use a good heavy-duty lithium complex grease, usually with a high moly content, because those pivot points take a massive amount of shear stress when that loader is carrying a full bucket of crushed rock. If you skip it, the pin gets galled up, and then you're looking at having to bring in a specialist to line-bore the whole joint, which takes days and costs a fortune. So you just have to dig in and deal with the mess, no matter how much you don't want to. 

But, uh... sorry, what was I saying? Oh, right, the house stuff. Yeah, no, I'm not avoiding any specific thoughts or anything. It's all just one big headache I'm stuck dealing with.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient experiences significant anxiety in specific social situations
doctor.question: Do you feel anxious when you're around other people, like at work or in social gatherings?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about social anxiety or anxiety around other people, which is not part of my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Anxious around other people? No, not really. I mean, I'm snapping at the apprentices, like I said, but that's just because my fuse is so short right now, not because they make me nervous. I've always been pretty comfortable around people, especially at the shop. It's a loud, chaotic environment, you know? Air compressors running, impacts hammering, radios blaring. You kind of have to yell just to be heard. 

Speaking of loud, we had this old Detroit Diesel Series 60 in the shop last week. A 12.7 liter, pre-EGR engine. Those things are legendary for being practically bulletproof, but man, they have a very distinct sound. People call it the "Detroit rattle." It's this sharp, clattering noise when they idle. Anyway, this guy brings his Freightliner Classic XL in, and the engine is just screaming. Sounded like someone threw a handful of bolts into a blender. Turned out, the bull gear in the front gear train was completely chewed up. The bull gear is this massive, heavy gear that drives the camshaft and the accessory drive. It's pressed onto a hub, and if the backlash isn't set perfectly when it's installed, or if the bearings start to fail, the teeth just grind themselves to dust. You have to pull the whole front cover off the engine, which means dropping the oil pan, pulling the radiator, the charge air cooler, the fan hub... it's a monumental job. And the whole time you're doing it, you're covered in this thick, black soot that just permeates your skin. You can wash your hands ten times with pumice soap and you'll still have a black ring around your fingernails for a week. 

But, uh, no. I don't feel anxious around people. Just tired. Just really, really tired of it all.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient has lost interest in activities they once enjoyed due to their current situation
doctor.question: Are there any activities that you used to enjoy but have lost interest in since you started receiving the foreclosure notices?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve been taken out of the high-risk repair bay at work, and I’ve stopped showing up for church volunteering, fitness classes, and truck-club outings I used to keep up with.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about activities I used to enjoy but have lost interest in, which corresponds to my functional impairment where I stopped showing up for church volunteering, fitness classes, and truck-club outings.

patient.answer:
Activities I used to enjoy? Yeah, I mean... pretty much all of them, honestly. I just don't have it in me right now. Like, I used to go to these fitness classes twice a week, and I was always volunteering at church, helping set up for events. And my truck club outings! We used to do these weekend meets, barbecue, talk shop... I haven't been to one in months. I just stopped showing up for all of it. 

Even at work, it's affecting me. They actually took me out of the high-risk repair bay. Which, honestly, I get. You can't be distracted when you're working under a suspended load or dealing with high-pressure hydraulics. Like last month, before they moved me, we had this massive excavator come in, a Hitachi ZX470. The boom cylinder was leaking hydraulic fluid everywhere. Now, to repack those cylinders, you're dealing with immense pressure. The hydraulic fluid in those systems can run upwards of 5,000 PSI. If you crack a fitting before relieving the pressure, that fluid can inject right through your skin, and then you're looking at emergency surgery to prevent amputation. It's no joke. You have to use these massive spanner wrenches to get the gland nut off the cylinder, and sometimes you have to heat it with an oxy-acetylene torch just to break the thread locker loose. And the seals themselves, the chevron packing, it's this incredibly stiff polyurethane. You have to soak them in hot oil just to make them pliable enough to stretch over the piston without tearing them. It's exacting work, and you really have to be on your game. 

But yeah, they moved me to the lighter stuff, doing basic PMs—preventative maintenance—on the smaller delivery box trucks. Oil changes, greasing chassis, checking brake pad thickness. It's boring, but I guess it's safer right now since my head's not fully in it. So, yeah, I've just dropped out of everything I used to do.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms are persistent and pervasive enough to indicate a specific adjustment disorder
doctor.question: Have you been feeling this overwhelmed and anxious every day since you started receiving the foreclosure notices?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about four months, ever since the foreclosure notices started coming in.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the timeline of the symptoms in relation to the stressor, which directly corresponds to the duration of the current episode.

patient.answer:
Every single day, yeah. It's been about four months now, right when those first notices started showing up in the mail. Just this constant weight on my chest, every morning I wake up. 

It reminds me of when we had to pull the transmission on an Allison 4500 RDS out of a refuse truck a few months back. Those garbage trucks, they just get beaten to death, stop-and-go all day, every day. The PTO—power take-off—is constantly engaging and disengaging to run the hydraulic compactor. Anyway, this thing came in and it wouldn't shift out of second gear. We dropped the pan, and the fluid looked like burnt coffee, full of clutch material. We had to drop the driveline, support the back of the engine, and use a heavy-duty transmission jack to lower this massive hunk of iron out from under the chassis. And when you crack the case open on an Allison, it's like a puzzle box of planetary gear sets, clutch packs, and the valve body. The valve body is the brain, full of these tiny little solenoids and shift valves. If even a speck of dirt gets in there, the valve sticks, and you lose a gear. We had to soak the whole assembly in solvent, blow out every single passage with compressed air, and test every solenoid with a multimeter to make sure the resistance was within spec. It's tedious, frustrating work, and you're just standing there under the lift for hours, your neck cramping up, transmission fluid dripping in your hair... 

But yeah, four months of this. Every day since the bank started sending those letters, I just feel completely overwhelmed.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of avoidance behaviors
doctor.question: Are you avoiding talking to anyone in particular about your foreclosure situation?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about avoiding talking to specific people about the foreclosure situation, which relates to avoidance behaviors. The provided symptom profiles do not include specific information about avoiding conversations or people.

patient.answer:
Avoiding anyone? Um... well, I haven't really told anyone at all, to be honest. It's not like I'm actively hiding from one specific person, I just... I don't want to talk about it with anyone. It's embarrassing, you know? 

Like, I don't want the guys at the shop knowing my business. We talk a lot of trash, but it's mostly about the equipment. Like yesterday, we were arguing over the best way to diagnose a DPF—diesel particulate filter—issue on a Cummins ISX15. Those things are a nightmare. The EPA regulations mandate all this aftertreatment stuff now, so you've got the DPF, the DOC, the SCR... it's a whole alphabet soup under the truck. Anyway, when a DPF clogs up with soot, the engine computer initiates an active regen, basically dumping raw fuel into the exhaust stream to burn the soot out. But if the seventh injector—the doser valve—is clogged, or if the differential pressure sensor is lying to the ECM, the regen fails, and the truck derates. It basically goes into limp mode, and the driver can't go over 5 miles an hour. So you hook up your laptop with the Cummins Insite software, and you're looking at all these parameters—exhaust gas temperatures, soot load percentages. Sometimes you have to force a parked regen, and the truck just sits there screaming at 1500 RPM for an hour, blowing out heat that could melt the asphalt. If that doesn't work, you have to physically pull the DPF down, which weighs like 80 pounds and is usually rusted solid to the v-band clamps, and send it out to be baked in a specialized kiln. It's a massive headache.

But yeah, I don't talk about the house stuff with them. Or my sister. Or anyone, really. I just keep it to myself.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a significant change in appetite
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in your appetite since you started receiving the foreclosure notices?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in appetite, which is a symptom of depression or anxiety, but it is not specifically listed in the patient's symptom profile for Adjustment Disorder.

patient.answer:
Changes in my appetite? Um... I don't think so. I haven't really noticed, honestly. I guess I'm eating about the same as usual. I still grab my regular sandwich from the lunch truck when it rolls into the yard every day. 

Actually, speaking of food trucks, we just had a massive refrigerated delivery truck in the shop a couple weeks ago that hauls for the local restaurants. A Freightliner M2 with a Thermo King T-880R reefer unit on the box. The driver came in panicking because the box wouldn't drop below 40 degrees, and he was hauling frozen seafood, so that's a huge liability. When you're dealing with those transport refrigeration units, it's a whole different ballgame than just heavy diesel. You're basically an HVAC tech on top of being a mechanic. 

I hooked up my manifold gauges to the suction and discharge service valves on the compressor, and the low-side pressure was pulling way down into a vacuum. That tells you right away there's either a massive leak in the system or a restriction. We had to break out the electronic leak detector and trace every single inch of the refrigerant lines. Turns out, the vibration from the road had caused a heavy wire loom to rub right through the liquid line going to the expansion valve. You can't just vent that stuff to fix it, either. You have to hook up a recovery machine and pull all the remaining R-404a refrigerant into a DOT-approved cylinder. If the EPA catches you venting hydrofluorocarbons, they will fine the shop tens of thousands of dollars. So you recover it, braze in a new section of copper tubing with a torch, swap out the liquid line filter drier, and then you have to pull a deep vacuum on the whole system with a two-stage pump down to like 500 microns to boil off any moisture before you can even think about weighing in the new charge. It took my entire shift just to get it blowing ice cold again. 

But, um... what were you asking? Oh, right, my eating. Yeah, no, my appetite is pretty much the same, I haven't noticed any changes there.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of avoidance behaviors related to the foreclosure situation
doctor.question: Are you avoiding talking to anyone in particular about your financial difficulties with the house?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about avoiding talking to people about financial difficulties, which is a repetition of a previous question about avoidance. The symptom profile does not contain specific information about avoidance behaviors, only about emotional/behavioral symptoms, timing relative to the stressor, functional impairment, and duration.

patient.answer:
Wait, didn't we just talk about that? Or... I guess you mean specifically about the money side of it. But yeah, like I said before, I'm not really hiding from anyone in particular. I just don't bring up the financial stuff or the house with anybody at all. It's just... money is so stressful right now. 

It's like that with the customers at the shop, too, honestly. Everyone's stressed about money and repair bills. We had this guy bring in a John Deere 544 wheel loader last week, and the main hydraulic implement pump was just whining like a banshee. When you're dealing with those variable displacement axial piston pumps, if the swashplate wears out or the brass slippers get scored up from contaminated fluid, the whole system just loses pressure. You try to curl a loaded bucket and it just completely stalls out. 

I had to tell the guy that to replace that pump, he was looking at easily eight, maybe ten grand just for the part alone. And getting it out is a total nightmare. You're belly-crawling under the cab, dealing with these massive high-pressure hydraulic lines. You have to be so careful, because if you don't bleed the residual pressure out of the accumulators first, that hydraulic fluid can shoot out and inject straight through your skin, which is a guaranteed trip to the ER and emergency surgery. We had to drain like fifty gallons of AW46 hydraulic oil into these massive drums, unbolt the drive shaft, and wrestle this eighty-pound hunk of steel out of the belly pan. And the whole time, the customer is standing around the bay complaining about our hourly labor rate. I'm just thinking, buddy, you want this thing lifting concrete jersey barriers or not? You can't cheap out on hydraulics. 

But, um... yeah. To answer your question again, no. I'm not avoiding anyone specifically about the finances. I just keep it all to myself.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the criteria for adjustment disorder with a specific focus on the presence of significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of functioning
doctor.question: Have you found it difficult to perform your job or maintain relationships since you started receiving the foreclosure notices?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve been taken out of the high-risk repair bay at work, and I’ve stopped showing up for church volunteering, fitness classes, and truck-club outings I used to keep up with.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulties performing my job or maintaining relationships, which directly corresponds to the functional impairment criterion.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, I guess it has been affecting things. Like at work, my foreman actually took me out of the high-risk repair bay recently. I guess I was just too distracted with the house stuff on my mind. And you really, really can't be distracted in the high-risk bay. That's where we handle the heavy suspension overhauls and the air brake chambers. 

People who just drive regular cars don't realize how dangerous commercial air brakes are. You've got these dual-chamber brake pots on the drive axles—one side is the service brake, and the other is the spring brake, which acts as the parking and emergency brake. There's a massive, heavy-duty steel coil spring inside that housing holding back like two or three thousand pounds of mechanical force. If you need to replace a ruptured rubber diaphragm inside, you absolutely have to manually cage that spring first. You use this special T-bolt that threads into the back of the chamber and compresses the spring safely. If you're not paying attention and you take off the metal clamp band while that spring is still under tension... man, that housing will explode like a literal bomb. It will take your head clean off your shoulders. We had a young tech a few years ago who didn't respect the spring tension, and the housing shot off and shattered his jaw and collarbone. So, you know, if your head isn't one hundred percent in the game, they won't let you near it. 

So I'm mostly just doing basic preventative maintenance right now. Oil changes, greasing chassis, that kind of thing. 

And outside of work... I don't know, I just don't have the energy for anyone. I've stopped showing up for my church volunteering, I dropped my fitness classes, and I haven't been to any of my truck-club outings either. We used to do these big weekend meetups, showing off custom glider kits. A lot of the folks run classic Peterbilt 389s with the extended hoods. You drop a pre-emission Caterpillar C15 engine in there, twin turbos, straight-pipe exhaust with eight-inch bullhauler stacks... they sound incredible when you hit the Jake brake coming down a grade. But I just haven't been going to those either. I just don't have it in me to keep up with any of it right now.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms, including persistent and pervasive feelings of anxiety, fear, and apprehension about the future, avoidance of social interactions and activities they once enjoyed, and significant distress or impairment in social or occupational functioning, are consistent with a diagnosis of Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) related to the foreclosure notices and financial stress. However, the lack of a clear traumatic stressor and the focus on anxiety and avoidance related to the foreclosure situation suggest that the diagnosis might be more accurately described as an adjustment disorder with anxiety.
